title: Iris: An AI-Driven Virtual Tutor For Computer Science Education
venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1 (ITiCSE 2024)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing scalable, personalized support for programming students in large computer science courses. The authors argue that general-purpose chatbots and standalone LLMs are not well suited for educational use because they often lack access to course-specific context and may reveal complete solutions, which can undermine learning. To address this, they introduce Iris, a chat-based virtual tutor integrated into the Artemis learning platform.

Iris is designed to support students working on programming exercises by using contextual information such as the exercise statement, the student’s code, automated feedback, and build logs. It is configured through prompt engineering to behave like an “excellent tutor” that gives subtle hints, counter-questions, and other calibrated assistance rather than full solutions. The system also filters irrelevant questions and uses a multi-step Chain-of-Thought interaction strategy with GPT-3.5-Turbo.

The study evaluates Iris through an online survey of students enrolled in three CS1-level undergraduate courses at the Technical University of Munich. Only students who had used Iris at least ten times were included in the main analysis, and the survey measured perceived usefulness, comfort asking questions, and subjective reliance. Results suggest that students generally view Iris positively as a helpful, engaging, and non-judgmental support tool, especially for routine programming exercises and lecture questions.

The main conclusion is that Iris is valued as a complementary resource rather than a replacement for human tutors. Students report high comfort using it and moderate reliance on it for coursework, but they remain confident in solving exam tasks without it. The authors conclude that AI tutoring can be effective when it is context-aware, carefully constrained, and positioned as supplemental to human instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed but qualitative/correlational survey study in a specific CS1 context, with no control group, randomization, or objective learning outcome measure. Internal validity is limited by self-report and selection into the ≥10-message subgroup.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest positive perceived impact on programming support, engagement, and comfort, but it does not demonstrate measured learning gains. Because outcomes are subjective and effect sizes are not reported, impact on learners is unclear beyond favorable perceptions.

interventions.use_case: chat-based virtual tutor integrated into the Artemis programming platform, using GPT-3.5-Turbo with chain-of-thought prompting, few-shot tutor role prompting, context-aware access to problem statements/code/test feedback, and guardrails to provide subtle hints and counter-questions rather than full solutions

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high comfort and safety using Iris, especially for asking questions without feeling judged. In the survey of 121 respondents (from 221 engaged users; 26% of the initial sample retained after filtering), 92% agreed they felt comfortable asking Iris questions without worrying about being judged, and 62% felt safe asking questions they would not ask a tutor or professor.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey responses on comfort/safety asking questions (Q6, Q7)

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived Iris as helping them understand programming concepts and supporting independent problem-solving through hints and counter-questions. In the surveyed group (n=121), 50% agreed that Iris improved their understanding of programming concepts, and 43% said solving programming exercises without Iris would be more challenging, suggesting perceived support for metacognitive/problem-solving development rather than direct solution provision.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perceptions of understanding programming concepts and reliance for solving exercises (Q3, Q10)

finding.finding_summary: Iris was viewed as engaging, though its influence on motivation was more mixed. Among n=121 respondents, 60% agreed that interacting with Iris made the learning process more engaging, while motivation responses were split (37% agree, 40% neutral, 23% disagree), indicating clearer gains in engagement than in motivation.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey responses on engagement and motivation (Q4, Q5)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students generally perceived Iris as effective for programming exercise support in CS1 settings. In n=121 survey respondents, 46% agreed Iris understood their queries well, 44% agreed it directly helped with exercise issues, and 50% agreed it improved understanding of programming concepts; however, the study is self-reported and does not measure objective performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived effectiveness on programming exercise assistance and concept understanding (Q1-Q3)
